title: De Grammatica
author: Augustine

passages.original: Omnia nomina tredecim literis terminantur: quinque vocalibus , a , e , i, o, II; sex semivocalibus , I, m, n, r, s, x; et duabus mutis, c, t. A masculino, ut Seneca, Catilina, Sulla, Uva, Cinna, Pansa; græca, Sosia, Pareta; afra, Jugurtha, Micipsa. A feminino, femina, musa, regula, norma, forma; et talia. A neu- Iro graeca sunt tantum , thema, schema, et unum nomen latinum fluminis, Turia; dicente Sallustio, Flumen Turia. (In Bello Jugurth). A communi, advena , convena , indigena, Trojugena; et talia. Ab epicœno , vipera, aquila, musca, locusta, ulula ; et talia. Diximus de a littera , nunc de e. Ab e littera vocali nullum latinum, nisi juncta pra positionc, masculinum invenitnr, ut proconsule, propraetore.
passages.english: All nouns end in thirteen letters: the five vowels a, e, i, o, u; six semivowels l, m, n, r, s, x; and two mutes, c, t. In a, [there are] masculines, such as Seneca, Catilina, Sulla, Uva, Cinna, Pansa; Greek ones, Sosia, Pareta; African ones, Jugurtha, Micipsa. Feminines: femina, musa, regula, norma, forma, and the like. Neuters are only Greek, thema, schema, and one Latin noun, [the name] of a river, Turia, as Sallust says, "The river Turia" (in the Jugurthine War). Common [gender]: advena, convena, indigena, Trojugena, and the like. Epicene: vipera, aquila, musca, locusta, ulula, and the like. We have spoken of the letter a; now of e. In the vowel e no Latin masculine is found, except when joined with a preposition, as proconsule, propraetore.
passages.notes: "II" read as u; "I" among the semivowels read as l. Uva as a masculine name is odd; perhaps a cognomen. The cited place "In Bello Jugurth." is an editorial reference; the phrase is not obviously in the Jugurtha.

passages.original: Hoc sono nominativi omnes casus declinantur : sic pluraliter; viri nihili, feminæ nihili, mancipia nihili. Ab epicœno nullum similiter exit in i. Ab o littera vocati nominativus terminatus masculino appellativo, ut ligo, ligonis. A proprio nomine, ut Cato, Cicero, Maro , Nero, Tubero , et cætera talia. A feminino appellativo, ut vertigo, indago, ferrago, siligo ( in Juvenali legitur ita : sed quæ mutalis inducitur atque fovetur Tot medicaminibus coctaeque siliginis offas Accipit et madidae, facies dicetur aut ulcus (Satira 6, v.
passages.english: With this sound of the nominative all the cases are declined; so too in the plural: viri nihili, feminae nihili, mancipia nihili. Of the epicene, likewise, none ends in i. A nominative ending in the vowel o: in a masculine common noun, as ligo, ligonis; in a proper noun, as Cato, Cicero, Maro, Nero, Tubero, and others like them; in a feminine common noun, as vertigo, indago, ferrago, siligo (in Juvenal it is read thus: "But what is changed and is coated and nursed with so many medicaments, and receives lumps of cooked and moist wheat-flour [siligo], is it to be called a face or a sore?" (Satire 6, lines
passages.notes: "vocati" read as vocali; "ferrago" probably for farrago. The Juvenal quotation is garbled in the text and conflates lines; translated approximately. The passage breaks off mid-reference.

passages.original: L littera nominativus exiens in masculinis appellativis, hic sal; in propriis, Sol. In femininis unum nomen matronae tantum , Tanaquil. In neutris, ut mel , fel. In . communibus, vigil, pugil : unde et Terentius de virgine, Pugilem esse aiunt (In Eun. act. 2, scen. 3, v. 24 ). In epicœnis nullum nomen est. M, nominativus exiens, in masculinis nullum latinum est. In femininis, Glycerium, Phanium , Dorcium, Philocomasium, In neutris .
passages.english: A nominative ending in the letter l: in masculine common nouns, hic sal; in proper nouns, Sol. In feminines only one noun, [the name] of a matron, Tanaquil. In neuters, as mel, fel. In common [gender], vigil, pugil: hence Terence too says of a girl, "They say she is a boxer" (Eunuch, act 2, scene 3, line 24). In epicenes there is no noun. A nominative ending in m: in masculines there is no Latin [noun]. In feminines, Glycerium, Phanium, Dorcium, Philocomasium. In neuters
passages.notes: Text breaks off at the end; the neuter examples follow in the next passage.

passages.original: hoc piper, v. o piper, A. ab hoc pipere. Ad hanc formam declinabis numero tantum singulari, ver : N. hoc ver, G. hujus veris, D. huic veri, A. hoc ver, v. o ver, ab hoc verr. Sic decl nabis hoc siler, ut ait Virgilius, Molle siter (Georg. lib. 2, v. 13). Similiter declinabis et juger. sed habet pluralem, ut jugcr jugera, secundnm antiquos qui dixerunt jugerum ; uber ubera, tuber tubcra : et in hæc, ut dixi, paucorum nomina sun!.
passages.english: V. o piper, Abl. ab hoc pipere. On this pattern you will decline, in the singular number only, ver: N. hoc ver, G. hujus veris, D. huic veri, Acc. hoc ver, V. o ver, Abl. ab hoc vere. So you will decline hoc siler, as Virgil says, "the soft osier" (Georgics book 2, line 13). Likewise you will decline juger too, but it has a plural, as juger, jugera, according to the ancients who said jugerum; uber, ubera; tuber, tubera: and in these, as I said, there are nouns of few [words].
passages.notes: "hoc piper" at the start (nominative) is repeated from the preceding paradigm; "verr" read as vere; "siter" as siler. Last clause "paucorum nomina sunt" is awkward, apparently 'these are the forms of only a few nouns'.

passages.original: ab bor et ab hac memore : et pluraliter, Nominativo bi et hae memores, G. horum et harum memorum. D. bis memoribus, A. hos et has memores, v. o memores. A. ab his memoribus. AdmiUit et neutrum, sed non in regula generis omnis, ut boc memor, andeet Virgilius: Tum si quod non aequo foedere amantes cane numen habet, justumque memorque precator. (Æneid. lib. 4, w. 520,521.) Pluralem non admittit, inde non cst generis omnis. Neque enim dicimus memora vel memoria numina. Similiter declinabis auctorem in nominativo singulari, hic et hæc auctor, ut ait Juno, Auctor ego audendi ( Id.
passages.english: Abl. ab hoc and ab hac memore; and in the plural, Nom. hi and hae memores, G. horum and harum memorum, D. his memoribus, Acc. hos and has memores, V. o memores, Abl. ab his memoribus. It also admits the neuter, but not according to the rule of all genders, as hoc memor; hence also Virgil: "Then, if any deity, just and mindful, has in its care lovers bound by an unequal pact, she prays [to it]." (Aeneid book 4, lines 520–521.) It does not admit a plural; hence it is not of all genders. For we do not say memora or memoria numina. Likewise you will decline auctor in the nominative singular, hic and haec auctor, as Juno says, "I [am] the author of daring" (ibid.
passages.notes: The Virgil quotation is garbled ("amantes cane numen" for "amantis curae numen"); translated in its evident sense. Text breaks off mid-reference.

passages.original: epicœnum autem cum articulo uno masculino communicat namen femininam, ut cum dico hic passer, sub ipso articulo qui sonat hic, intelligitur et femina. Sic in articulo generis neutri, quod est hoc pecus : sub articulo qui sonat hoc, intelligitur et femina, ut Virgilius ait, Lenta salix felo pecori (Eclog. 5, v. 83). Et in pecore licct sit gcnus neutrum, auditur illic et genus femininum, cum dixit, fclo pccori, id est gravido.
passages.english: The epicene, however, shares the noun with a single masculine article [while also covering] the female: as when I say hic passer, under the very article that sounds hic the female too is understood. So with the article of the neuter gender, as hoc pecus: under the article that sounds hoc the female too is understood, as Virgil says, "the pliant willow to the pregnant flock" (Eclogue 5, line 83). And in pecus, although it is neuter gender, the feminine gender is also heard there, when he said feto pecori, that is, pregnant.
passages.notes: "namen femininam" probably corrupt for 'nomen, et feminam'; translated accordingly. "felo/fclo pccori" read as feto pecori (Virgil's text actually belongs to Eclogue 3).

passages.original: Ideo pronomen dicitur, quia vice fungitur nominis: ut ille, iste, ipse. Nam quomodo dicendo nomen explicamus personam, ut Virgilius; sic pronomina propric cjusdem potestatis suut, cum tacito nomine dicimus, Hic fecit, iste fecit. Pronomina aut finita sunt, aut infinita, aut minus quam finita. Finita sunt dux notam certam personam, ut ego.
passages.english: It is called a pronoun because it performs the function of a noun, as ille, iste, ipse. For just as by saying a noun we make a person clear, as "Virgil", so pronouns are properly of the same force, when, with the noun left unsaid, we say "This man did it", "that man did it". Pronouns are either definite, or indefinite, or less than definite. Definite are those that mark a definite person, as ego.

passages.original: Iste, similiter et ipse, ad formam superiorem declinabis, tam ad genera quam etiam ad numeros. Sane quaestio est in boc pronotnine ipse, quare cum istud et illud in genere neutro dicimus, dicamus ipsum, ut ait Virgilius. Atque ipsum corpus amici (Æneid. lib. i, v. 490): non dixit,ipsud. Sed hanc quastio solvitur hoc modo : Antiqui enim magis ipsus dicebant in nominativo singulari generis masculini quam ipse. Hanc antiquitatis rationem attendentes ariis scriptores, pronomen hoc ad formam nominis transtulerunt : ut quomodo iii nomme jublus, justa, justum dicimus, et perfectus, perfecta, perfectum;
passages.english: Iste, and likewise ipse, you will decline on the pattern above, both in genders and in numbers. There is indeed a question about this pronoun ipse: why, when we say istud and illud in the neuter gender, we say ipsum, as Virgil says, "and the very body of his friend" (Aeneid book 1, line 490); he did not say ipsud. But this question is solved in this way: the ancients said ipsus in the nominative singular of the masculine gender rather than ipse. Writers of the arts, attending to this reasoning from antiquity, transferred this pronoun to the form of a noun, so that just as in a noun we say justus, justa, justum, and perfectus, perfecta, perfectum;

passages.original: Nominativo quis, c. cujus, D. cui, A. quem, v. o qui, A. a quo : et pluraliter, N. qui, c. quorum, D. quis vel quibus ( ut Virgilius, Quis ante ora patrum (Ibid. 99), A. quos, v. o qui, A. a quibus. Feminino genere, N. quæ, G. cujus, D. cui, A. quam, v. oqune, A. a qua : ei pluraliter, N. quae, G. quarum, D quis, A. quas, v. o quæ.
passages.english: Nom. quis, G. cujus, D. cui, Acc. quem, V. o qui, Abl. a quo; and in the plural, N. qui, G. quorum, D. quis or quibus (as Virgil, "[for whom] before the faces of their fathers" (ibid. 99)), Acc. quos, V. o qui, Abl. a quibus. In the feminine gender, N. quae, G. cujus, D. cui, Acc. quam, V. o quae, Abl. a qua; and in the plural, N. quae, G. quarum, D. quis, Acc. quas, V. o quae.
passages.notes: Virgil, Aeneid 1.95, "quis ante ora patrum" ("to whom"); reference given as 99.

passages.original: Verba quatuor modis accipimus : priino modo, cum verba pro fallaciis accipimus, cum dicimus, verla illi dedit, fefellit eum : uude Terentius dixit, Cui verba dare difficile est (And. act. i, scen. 5, v. 6). Sccundo modo, verba pro oratione dicimus, verba fccisse Ciceroncm in curia. Tertio modo, verba dicimus pro vulgaribus sententiis quæ proverbia dicuntux, ut Terentius dixit : veruli illud verbum vulgo cst quod dici solet. (rerent., and. ad. 2, scen. i, i. 15). Quarto modo, verba dicimus hæc quæ decurrimus tum temporibus et personis, ut clamo, clamas, clamat. llic et personæ sunt tres, ut clamo ego, clamas tu, clamat ille ;
passages.english: We take verba [words] in four ways. In the first way, when we take verba for deceptions, when we say verba illi dedit, [meaning] he deceived him: hence Terence said, "whom it is difficult to deceive" (Andria act 1, scene 5, line 6). In the second way, we say verba for a speech: [that] Cicero made verba in the senate house. In the third way, we say verba for common sayings, which are called proverbs, as Terence said: "That saying is true which is commonly said" (Terence, Andria act 2, scene 1, line 15). In the fourth way, we call verba those which we run through by tenses and persons, as clamo, clamas, clamat. Here there are three persons, as clamo ego, clamas tu, clamat ille;
passages.notes: The Terence line is quoted with a garbled word ("veruli" for verum).

passages.original: Sic ergo observemus, ut nec euphoniam applicemus ad regulam, aut euphoniam rejiciamus. Nain euphonia, id est suavitas bene sonandi admissa est ad latinum sermonem, ut aspera temperet: et ab arte ex ratione recessum est, ubi asperitas offendebat auditum. Sic Cicero ait: Impetratum est a ratione, ut peccare suavitatis causa liceret. Sed tamen in paucis admissa euphonia est. Nam ratio locuples estet viris latinissimis. Sanecirca has regulas auctoritas ausa est, et in paucis praesumpsit, ut diceret Cicero, humaniter, cum humane dicere debuit: et Terentius, Vitam parce ac duriter agebat (in Andria act.
passages.english: Let us therefore observe [this], so that we neither apply euphony to the rule nor reject euphony. For euphony, that is, the sweetness of sounding well, has been admitted into the Latin language to temper harsh [forms]; and there has been a departure from the rule of the art, on rational grounds, where harshness offended the ear. So Cicero says: "It was obtained from reason that it should be permitted to err for the sake of sweetness." But nevertheless euphony has been admitted in few cases. For reason is rich [enough] for the most Latin of men. Indeed, authority has made bold concerning these rules, and in a few cases has presumed, so that Cicero said humaniter when he ought to have said humane; and Terence, "He led his life sparingly and hardly (duriter)" (in the Andria, act
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Nain' as 'Nam', 'estet' as 'est et', 'Sanecirca' as 'Sane circa'. The passage breaks off mid-reference; the citation continues in the following text.

passages.original: Sunt adverbia quantitatis, ut longe, late. Qualitatis, ut bene, male. Adverbia non solum ab appellationibus transeunt, hoc est a nominibus appellativis, ut a pulchro, pulchre; sed a propriis, ut Tullius, Tułłiane. A pronominibus etiam, a meo, tuo, meatim, tuatim : a verbis quoque, ut a curro cursim. Deprehenduntur ex utroque, ut pedetentim a pede et tento, id est a nomine simul et verbo. Sunt ctiam adverbia, qune utrum a nomine transeant, an a verbo incertum est, ut furtim.
passages.english: There are adverbs of quantity, such as longe (far), late (widely); of quality, such as bene (well), male (badly). Adverbs are derived not only from appellatives, that is from common nouns, as pulchre from pulcher, but also from proper nouns, as Tulliane from Tullius. [They come] also from pronouns, as meatim, tuatim from meus, tuus; from verbs too, as cursim from curro. Some are found [to be formed] from both, as pedetentim from pes (foot) and tento, that is, from a noun and a verb together. There are also adverbs of which it is uncertain whether they derive from a noun or from a verb, such as furtim (stealthily).

passages.original: Sed ex iis quaedam per syncopem euphoniæ causa dicimus, ut audacter, difficulter, sapicnter et constanter. Sunt adverbia communia cum aliis partibus orationis. Nominibus sunt communia, ut ait SallustiuS : Fatso queritur de natura sua genus humanum (In Bello Jugurth.): pro false. Virgilius, Et pede terram crebro ferit (Georg. lib. 3, v. 500): et, Multa Jovem manibus supplex orasse supinis. (Æneid. lib. 4, r. 205.) Conjunctioni ut, quando adverbium secum est, plura significat.
passages.english: But some of these we say with syncope for the sake of euphony, such as audacter, difficulter, sapienter and constanter. There are adverbs shared with other parts of speech. They are shared with nouns, as Sallust says: "The human race complains falsely (falso) of its nature" (in the Jugurthine War), for false. Virgil: "And strikes the earth with frequent (crebro) foot" (Georgics 3.500); and: "Is said to have prayed much (multa) to Jupiter, a suppliant with upturned hands" (Aeneid 4.205). With a conjunction, ut, when it is an adverb, signifies several things.
passages.notes: 'Fatso' read as 'Falso'. The last sentence is awkwardly transmitted; sense appears to be that ut, shared with the conjunction, has several adverbial meanings, listed in what follows.

passages.original: Recipiunt et diminutionem, ut meliuscule. Quanquam comparationem recipiunt et diminutionem, et quæ a se nascuntur, ut naper, nuperrime. Adverbiis omnibus præpositio separatim adjici non debet, quanquam lectum sit, ab hinc, apud Terentium, Interia mulier quædam nb hinc triennium (in mdria,act. i, scen. i, v.40.) Et apud Virgilium, Exinde per altum mittimur Elysium (Æneid. lib. 6, vv. 743, 744). Et dehinc : ut, Dehinc talia fatur (Id. lib. 1, v. 256) : et, Deinde feraces plantœ immittuntur (Georg. lib. 2, vv. 79, 80): quæ omnia, et si qua alia sunt similia, ut proinde;
passages.english: They also admit the diminutive, as meliuscule (somewhat better). Though they admit comparison and the diminutive, [so do] also those that arise from themselves, as nuper, nuperrime. A preposition ought not to be added separately to any adverb, although ab hinc has been read in Terence: "A certain woman died three years ago (ab hinc)" (Andria 1.1.40). And in Virgil: "Thence (exinde) we are sent through wide Elysium" (Aeneid 6.743–744). And dehinc, as: "Then (dehinc) he speaks such words" (Aeneid 1.256); and: "Then (deinde) fruitful shoots are inserted" (Georgics 2.79–80). All of these, and any others like them, such as proinde,
passages.notes: 'naper' read as 'nuper'. The second sentence seems garbled in the transmitted text; translation is tentative. The final sentence continues in the following text.

passages.original: Est unum participium praterili temporis in uus, quod exire debuit per unum u, non per, duo. Nam ubi geminata u littera nominativus cst, Homen est, non pariicipium, ut fatuus, ingenuus, arduus, carduus, exiguus, belluus, ut Cicero dixit In us, ut talium contra regulam participiorum, mortuus . putatur esse participium, sed in vim regulamque nominis conversum cst.
passages.english: There is one participle of the past tense in -uus, which ought to have ended with a single u, not two. For where the nominative has a doubled letter u, it is a noun, not a participle, as fatuus, ingenuus, arduus, carduus, exiguus, belluus, as Cicero said. Among [forms] in -us, as one of such participles contrary to the rule, mortuus is thought to be a participle, but it has been turned into the force and rule of a noun.
passages.notes: Text is corrupt in places ('In us, ut talium'); 'belluus' is doubtful. The point seems to be that mortuus is treated as a noun-like adjective.

passages.original: Si autem in uno eodemque loco, ablativum: ut curro in foro, curro in campo : sic ambulo in foro, et ambulo in campo. Si de alio loco ambulamus in forum, accusativum tenemus. Si in eodem loco ambulamus , ablativum tenemus, ut ambulo in foro : sic, cadit in forum, et cadit in furo. Virgilius : . Ingrediturque solo, et ea; ut inter nubila condit. (Aneid. lib. 4, v. i77.) III est, Jn arvis altius ingreditur (Georg. lib. 3, vv. 75, 76), id est ambulat : vides molum esse, et tamen ablativum sibi vindicare;
passages.english: But if [the motion is] in one and the same place, [it takes] the ablative: as curro in foro, curro in campo (I run in the forum, in the field); so ambulo in foro and ambulo in campo. If we walk from another place into the forum, we use the accusative. If we walk in the same place, we use the ablative, as ambulo in foro; so cadit in forum and cadit in foro. Virgil: "And she walks upon the ground, and hides her head among the clouds" (Aeneid 4.177). Likewise: "steps higher in the fields" (Georgics 3.75–76), that is, walks: you see that it is motion, and yet it claims the ablative for itself;
passages.notes: Virgil quotation garbled in the scan ('et ea; ut inter nubila condit' for 'et caput inter nubila condit'). 'III est' probably 'Item'.

passages.original: Kx hac ergo foima intelligimus quomodo declinemus : hic duumvir, quasi duorum hominum unus vir. Sic triumvir, Uium hominum unus vir. Ergo hic admisit genitivum. Jam quatuor ubi indecl nabile est, quatuorviri dicimus, vel quinqueviri, vel sexviri. Unde Lucanus, Septemvirque epulis : pro genitivo posuit, septem. A ducentis usque ad nongentos declinantur nomina numerorum , ut hi ducenti, hæ ducentæ, neutro ducenta : mille, declinabile est.
passages.english: From this pattern, then, we understand how we should decline: hic duumvir, as if one man of two men. So triumvir, one man of three men. So this admitted the genitive. Now with quattuor, where it is indeclinable, we say quattuorviri, or quinqueviri, or sexviri. Hence Lucan, "and septemvir for the feasts": he used septem for the genitive. From two hundred to nine hundred the numerals are declined, as hi ducenti, hae ducentae, neuter ducenta; mille is declinable.
passages.notes: 'Uium' read as 'trium'. The final claim that mille is declinable may be corrupt (one would expect 'indeclinabile').
